question: Assertion (A): Under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, a proposed vendee who has taken possession under an unregistered agreement to sell can file a suit for declaration of title against the vendor. Reason (R): The doctrine of Part Performance in India confers equitable title upon the transferee once possession is transferred and consideration is paid.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are false
explanation: In India, Section 53A does not confer any title, legal or equitable, on the transferee. As established in 'Prabodh Kumar Das v. Dantmara Tea Co.', the right conferred by Section 53A is a right of defense only. It can only be used as a shield to defend possession, never as a sword to claim declaration of title.
trick: NET Law Trap: Section 53A (Part Performance) in India can ONLY be used as a SHIELD (to defend possession), not as a SWORD (to claim title or evict others)!
tip: Section 53A confers no equitable title; it is merely a defensive right.

question: Which landmark English case forms the jurisprudential bedrock for Section 52 (Lis Pendens), establishing that the doctrine does not rest upon the doctrine of constructive notice, but upon public policy and necessity?
options: Maddison v. Alderson
Bellamy v. Sabine
Ramsden v. Dyson
Cooper v. Phibbs
answer: Bellamy v. Sabine
explanation: In 'Bellamy v. Sabine' (1857), Lord Cranworth explicitly clarified that Lis Pendens rests on necessity and public policy to prevent multiplicity of suits, not on the doctrine of notice. If alienations during litigation were allowed, litigation would never come to an end.
trick: Historical Trap: Many assume Lis Pendens works because a pending suit acts as 'notice' to the world. 'Bellamy v. Sabine' expressly rejects the notice theory in favor of necessity.
tip: Lis Pendens (S.52) rests on necessity and public policy, not constructive notice.

question: Assertion (A): Section 43 (Feeding the Grant by Estoppel) applies even if the transferor's interest at the time of the transfer was a mere spes successionis under Section 6(a). Reason (R): In 'Jumma Masjid v. Kodimaniandra', the Supreme Court held that Section 43 operates on the representation made by the transferor, and Section 6(a) does not override this equitable estoppel.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
explanation: The Supreme Court in 'Jumma Masjid' harmonized Section 6(a) and Section 43. If a person transfers a mere expectancy (spes successionis) explicitly stating they have a present title, Section 43 applies when they later acquire the title. The transferee is protected by estoppel.
trick: Statutory Conflict Trap: Section 6(a) bans transferring spes successionis. However, if the transferor fraudulently claims to have PRESENT title, Section 43's estoppel bypasses the Section 6(a) bar.
tip: S.43 estoppel overrides the S.6(a) ban if a false representation of present title exists.

question: Under Section 41 (Ostensible Owner), which of the following is NOT an essential prerequisite for a transferee to claim protection against the real owner?
options: The transfer must be for consideration.
The transferee must have acted in good faith.
The real owner must have executed a registered power of attorney in favor of the ostensible owner.
The transferee must have taken reasonable care to ascertain that the transferor had power to make the transfer.
answer: The real owner must have executed a registered power of attorney in favor of the ostensible owner.
explanation: Section 41 requires the ostensible owner to hold the property with the express or implied consent of the real owner. A formal registered power of attorney is not mandatory; implied consent through conduct or inaction is sufficient to invoke the doctrine.
trick: Evidentiary Trap: Consent under Section 41 can be purely implied. Demanding a formal registered PoA confuses Agency law with the equitable doctrine of Ostensible Ownership.
tip: Consent for ostensible ownership can be implied; registered authorization is not required.

question: Following the 2001 amendment to the Registration Act, 1908, how does an unregistered agreement to sell affect the defense of Part Performance under Section 53A of the TPA?
options: It remains a valid defense as Section 53A operates independently of the Registration Act.
The defense of Section 53A is entirely barred if the document containing the contract is unregistered.
The defense is valid only if the transferee pays a penalty to the Sub-Registrar.
The defense is barred only for commercial properties, not residential ones.
answer: The defense of Section 53A is entirely barred if the document containing the contract is unregistered.
explanation: The Registration and Other Related Laws (Amendment) Act, 2001 amended Section 17(1A) of the Registration Act and Section 53A of the TPA. Now, the documents containing contracts to transfer for consideration must be registered. If unregistered, they shall have no effect for the purposes of Section 53A.
trick: Amendment Trap: Pre-2001, an unregistered agreement was the classic trigger for S.53A. Post-2001, lack of registration completely kills the S.53A defense.
tip: Post-2001, an unregistered agreement to sell cannot trigger S.53A Part Performance.

question: Assertion (A): Section 52 (Lis Pendens) makes any transfer of property during a pending suit void ab initio. Reason (R): The purpose of Section 52 is to paralyze the power of alienation during litigation to preserve the court's jurisdiction.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
answer: A is false but R is true
explanation: Assertion (A) is false because a transfer pendente lite is NOT void ab initio. It is perfectly valid between the transferor and transferee, but it is subservient to the final decree of the court. The transferee is bound by the decree as if they were a party to the suit.
trick: Effect Trap: Lis Pendens does not nullify the transfer; it makes it subject to the outcome of the litigation. The transfer is 'voidable' against the successful decree-holder.
tip: Lis pendens does not make transfers void; it makes them subject to the decree.

question: A fraudulently represents to B that he is the owner of C's estate and sells it to B. C subsequently dies, and A inherits the estate as C's sole heir. Before B exercises his option under Section 43 to claim the property, A sells it to D, who buys it in good faith, for consideration, and without notice of B's prior claim. Who gets the property?
options: B, because Section 43 operates automatically the moment A inherits the property.
B, because his earlier contract takes chronological precedence over D's contract.
D, because the exception in Section 43 protects a subsequent bona fide purchaser for value without notice.
The property escheats to the State due to A's initial fraud.
answer: D, because the exception in Section 43 protects a subsequent bona fide purchaser for value without notice.
explanation: Section 43 states that the subsequent acquisition feeds the grant 'at the option of the transferee' (B). It is not automatic. Furthermore, the explicit proviso to S.43 protects a subsequent transferee (D) who takes in good faith, for consideration, and without notice of the option existing.
trick: Vesting Trap: The title does NOT vest automatically in the first transferee. It requires exercise of option, and fails if a bona fide purchaser steps in first.
tip: S.43 requires the transferee to exercise their option; bona fide purchasers are protected.

question: Which of the following suits does NOT attract the doctrine of Lis Pendens under Section 52?
options: A suit for specific performance of a contract to sell immovable property.
A suit for partition of a joint Hindu family property.
A suit for the recovery of a general money debt where the plaintiff attaches the defendant's property before judgment.
A suit for foreclosure of a mortgage.
answer: A suit for the recovery of a general money debt where the plaintiff attaches the defendant's property before judgment.
explanation: Section 52 applies only to suits in which any right to immovable property is 'directly and specifically in question'. A general suit for money, even if it involves an attachment before judgment, does not put the title of the property directly in question.
trick: Attachment Trap: Attachment restricts alienation under CPC, but it does not invoke Lis Pendens (S.52 TPA) because the suit itself is not ABOUT the property's title.
tip: Lis pendens requires the property right to be directly and specifically in question.

question: In the context of Section 41 (Ostensible Owner), how has the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 practically impacted its application?
options: It has expanded Section 41 to include movable properties.
It has rendered Section 41 largely obsolete because real owners can no longer claim property held benami, thus eliminating the traditional ostensible owner conflict.
It mandated that all ostensible ownership arrangements must be registered.
It exempted family members entirely from the application of Section 41.
answer: It has rendered Section 41 largely obsolete because real owners can no longer claim property held benami, thus eliminating the traditional ostensible owner conflict.
explanation: Section 41 traditionally protected purchasers from real owners who had parked property in a benamidar's name. Since the Benami Act 1988 prohibits real owners from recovering benami property, the real owner cannot challenge the ostensible owner's title anyway, making Section 41 practically redundant in benami contexts.
trick: Statutory Interaction Trap: The Benami Act destroyed the foundational scenario of S.41. If the real owner can't sue the benamidar, they certainly can't sue the transferee.
tip: Benami Act 1988 severely restricts S.41 by barring real owners from claiming benami property.

question: Assertion (A): Under Section 53A, the transferee must have performed or be willing to perform his part of the contract. Reason (R): If a transferee takes possession but subsequently defaults on paying the balance consideration, he can still retain possession using Section 53A because possession was lawfully acquired initially.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: A is true but R is false
explanation: Assertion (A) is true; continuous willingness to perform is a mandatory statutory condition. Reason (R) is false; if the transferee defaults on the balance payment, they lose the 'willingness to perform'. Section 53A is an equitable relief; defaulting destroys this equity, and the transferor can evict them.
trick: Temporal Equity Trap: Willingness to perform is not a one-time act at the time of taking possession. It must be a continuous state of mind up to the conclusion of the contract.
tip: Willingness to perform under S.53A must be continuous; defaulting destroys the defense.

question: A suit is dismissed by the trial court. The plaintiff files an appeal 30 days later within the limitation period. During this 30-day gap, the defendant sells the property to X. Does the doctrine of Lis Pendens apply to X?
options: No, because at the exact moment of sale, no suit or proceeding was pending.
Yes, because Section 52 explicitly states that the pendency of a suit includes the period between a decree and the filing of an appeal.
No, Section 52 only applies to trial proceedings, not appellate proceedings.
Yes, but only if the appellate court grants a specific stay order retroactively.
answer: Yes, because Section 52 explicitly states that the pendency of a suit includes the period between a decree and the filing of an appeal.
explanation: The Explanation to Section 52 clarifies that the pendency of a suit commences from the presentation of the plaint and continues until the suit or proceeding has been disposed of by a final decree, including the time available for filing an appeal.
trick: Limitation Gap Trap: A suit is deemed to be continuously pending during the limitation period for an appeal. A sale during this gap is hit by Lis Pendens.
tip: Lis pendens continues during the limitation period for filing an appeal.

question: For Section 43 (Feeding the Grant by Estoppel) to apply, what is the fundamental difference regarding the transferor's misrepresentation compared to the English doctrine of Estoppel?
options: English law requires the misrepresentation to be in writing, whereas Indian law allows oral misrepresentation.
English law requires the representation to be fraudulent, whereas Section 43 applies whether the representation was fraudulent or merely erroneous.
Indian law requires the transferee to be completely ignorant of the defect in title, whereas English law protects even a complicit transferee.
There is no difference; Section 43 is an exact replica of the English doctrine.
answer: English law requires the representation to be fraudulent, whereas Section 43 applies whether the representation was fraudulent or merely erroneous.
explanation: Section 43 of the TPA broadens the English equitable doctrine. It explicitly uses the words 'fraudulently or erroneously represents'. An innocent mistake regarding authority to transfer still binds the transferor once they acquire the title.
trick: Doctrinal Nuance Trap: 'Erroneous' representation is sufficient in India. The transferor cannot escape S.43 by claiming they made an honest mistake about their title.
tip: S.43 applies to both fraudulent and erroneous representations of title.

question: In which of the following scenarios can a transferee NOT invoke the doctrine of Part Performance (Section 53A) to defend their possession?
options: The contract is in writing but not registered.
The contract is oral, but the transferee has paid the full consideration and taken possession.
The transferee was already in possession as a tenant and continued in possession, but paid a token advance towards the purchase.
The written contract is signed by the transferor but not by the transferee.
answer: The contract is oral, but the transferee has paid the full consideration and taken possession.
explanation: Section 53A strictly requires a contract 'in writing signed by him or on his behalf'. Unlike the English doctrine of part performance (Maddison v. Alderson), Indian law absolutely rejects oral contracts for invoking Section 53A, regardless of payment or possession.
trick: English vs Indian Law Trap: English equity allows part performance for oral contracts. Indian statutory law (S.53A) mandates a written and signed contract without exception.
tip: Section 53A absolutely requires a written contract; oral contracts are excluded.

question: Assertion (A): The doctrine of Lis Pendens does not apply if the suit is collusive in nature. Reason (R): A collusive suit is a sham proceeding where there is no real contest between the parties, engineered solely to defraud a third-party purchaser.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
explanation: Section 52 explicitly states that it applies to any suit or proceeding which is 'not collusive'. A collusive suit is a fraudulent arrangement between the plaintiff and defendant to defeat the rights of a transferee. Equity and public policy deny the protection of S.52 to such sham litigations.
trick: Exception Trap: Lis pendens is an absolute rule, but 'collusive suits' are the statutory exception. The suit must be genuinely contentious.
tip: Lis pendens (S.52) does not apply to collusive (sham) suits.

question: A, a minor, inherits an estate. B, his uncle, manages the estate and sells it to C, claiming to be the owner. C buys in good faith after checking the municipal tax receipts which are in B's name. A attains majority and sues C to recover the property. Can C successfully invoke Section 41 (Ostensible Owner)?
options: Yes, because C acted in good faith and B was the apparent owner.
No, because municipal tax receipts do not constitute proof of title for reasonable inquiry.
No, because A, being a minor, was legally incapable of giving express or implied consent to B holding himself out as the owner.
Yes, because family management creates a presumption of ostensible ownership.
answer: No, because A, being a minor, was legally incapable of giving express or implied consent to B holding himself out as the owner.
explanation: Section 41 requires that the ostensible owner acts with the 'consent, express or implied' of the real owner. A minor lacks the legal capacity to consent. Therefore, a minor's property cannot be alienated by someone claiming to be an ostensible owner, and Section 41 protection fails.
trick: Capacity to Consent Trap: Good faith of the transferee is irrelevant if the foundational requirement—consent of a legally competent real owner—is missing.
tip: A minor cannot give consent; hence S.41 (Ostensible Owner) cannot apply against a minor.

question: X transfers his property to Y. However, X tells Y, 'I do not have the title right now, but my father is dying, and I will inherit it tomorrow.' Y buys it anyway. The father dies, X inherits the property. Y sues X under Section 43. What is the outcome?
options: Y wins because X subsequently acquired the title.
Y wins because X received consideration for the transfer.
X wins because Section 43 does not apply when the transferee knows the truth about the defect in title.
X wins because the transfer violates the rule against perpetuities.
answer: X wins because Section 43 does not apply when the transferee knows the truth about the defect in title.
explanation: Section 43 requires an 'erroneous or fraudulent representation' upon which the transferee relied. If the transferee knows the truth (that the transferor has no title but a mere spes successionis), there is no misrepresentation to rely upon. Estoppel cannot exist when the truth is known to both parties.
trick: Knowledge Trap: Estoppel requires reliance on a misrepresentation. If the buyer knows the seller lacks title, Section 43 collapses.
tip: S.43 fails if the transferee had knowledge of the transferor's defective title.

question: Under the doctrine of Lis Pendens (Section 52), if an alienation is made during the pendency of a suit, what is the exact legal status of the transferee regarding the final decree?
options: The transferee must be formally impleaded as a party to the suit to be bound by the decree.
The transferee is bound by the decree irrespective of whether they were impleaded or had notice of the suit.
The transferee can challenge the decree on the grounds of lack of notice.
The decree is void against the transferee unless the court explicitly mentions the alienation.
answer: The transferee is bound by the decree irrespective of whether they were impleaded or had notice of the suit.
explanation: The core of Section 52 is that a transferee pendente lite is bound by the outcome of the litigation just as if they were a party to the suit. They do not need to be impleaded, nor is lack of notice a defense. They step into the shoes of the transferor.
trick: Impleadment Trap: A pendente lite purchaser has no absolute right to be impleaded (Order 22 Rule 10 CPC applies, which is discretionary). They are bound regardless.
tip: Transferee pendente lite is bound by the decree even without impleadment or notice.

question: Assertion (A): Section 53A (Part Performance) can be invoked against a subsequent transferee who purchases the property from the original vendor. Reason (R): The equity of part performance creates a right in rem against the whole world.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: A is false but R is true
explanation: Wait, let's analyze carefully. Assertion (A) is true in part, BUT S.53A has a proviso: it does not apply against a subsequent transferee for value without notice. Reason (R) is completely false; S.53A does NOT create a right in rem, it creates an equity in personam. Therefore, both are technically false in the absolute sense, but standard legal logic dictates S.53A is not a right in rem. Let's provide the exact answer: Both A and R are false.
trick: Right in Rem Trap: Part performance creates a statutory equity enforceable against the transferor and persons claiming under him, but it is NOT a right in rem (it fails against a bona fide purchaser without notice).
tip: S.53A creates an equity in personam, failing against a bona fide purchaser without notice.

question: In 'Ramcoomar Koondoo v. John and Maria McQueen', the Privy Council laid down the foundational principles for which section of the Transfer of Property Act?
options: Section 41 (Ostensible Owner)
Section 43 (Feeding the Grant by Estoppel)
Section 52 (Lis Pendens)
Section 53A (Part Performance)
answer: Section 41 (Ostensible Owner)
explanation: The landmark 1872 Privy Council decision in 'Ramcoomar Koondoo' is the genesis of Section 41. It held that it is a principle of natural equity that where one man allows another to hold himself out as the owner of an estate, he cannot later recover it from a bona fide purchaser for value without notice.
trick: Case Mapping Trap: Match 'Bellamy v Sabine' to S.52, 'Maddison v Alderson' to S.53A, and 'Ramcoomar Koondoo' strictly to S.41 Ostensible Owner.
tip: Ramcoomar Koondoo is the landmark case for S.41 (Ostensible Owner).

question: A Hindu father gifts his self-acquired property to his son, mistakenly believing he had already completed the registration. The son takes possession. Later, the father formally registers the title in his own name. Can the son invoke Section 43 to compel the father to pass the valid title to him?
options: Yes, because it is a transfer between blood relatives.
Yes, because the son took physical possession based on an erroneous representation.
No, because Section 43 does not apply to gratuitous transfers (gifts).
No, because Section 43 only applies to ancestral property.
answer: No, because Section 43 does not apply to gratuitous transfers (gifts).
explanation: Section 43 explicitly states: 'Where a person fraudulently or erroneously represents that he is authorized to transfer certain immoveable property and professes to transfer such property FOR CONSIDERATION...'. It does not apply to gifts or gratuitous transfers.
trick: Consideration Trap: Estoppel under Section 43 strictly requires consideration. A donee of a gift cannot force the donor to 'feed the grant' if the donor subsequently acquires title.
tip: Section 43 (Feeding the Grant) strictly requires consideration; it never applies to gifts.

question: During the pendency of a mortgage foreclosure suit, the mortgagor leases out the property to a tenant for a 10-year term. The mortgagee obtains the final decree and seeks eviction. Can the tenant claim protection under rent control laws to defeat the mortgagee's decree?
options: Yes, because rent control laws override the Transfer of Property Act.
No, because the creation of a lease pendente lite is an alienation hit by Section 52, making the tenant bound by the foreclosure decree.
Yes, because leasing is a normal management act, not an alienation of title.
No, because Section 52 only applies to outright sales, not leases.
answer: No, because the creation of a lease pendente lite is an alienation hit by Section 52, making the tenant bound by the foreclosure decree.
explanation: Section 52 prohibits the property from being 'transferred or otherwise dealt with'. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that creating a lease pendente lite is 'otherwise dealing with' the property. The tenant is bound by the decree and cannot claim statutory tenant protections against the decree-holder.
trick: Lease as Alienation Trap: Lis pendens applies not just to sales, but to leases, mortgages, and any other creation of rights that affect the decree-holder.
tip: Creating a lease during litigation is hit by S.52; the tenant is bound by the decree.

question: Which of the following acts by a proposed transferee, who is already in possession of the property as a tenant, is sufficient to constitute 'an act in furtherance of the contract' under Section 53A?
options: Continuing to pay the regular monthly rent.
Making structural alterations to the property with the explicit permission of the owner pursuant to the agreement to sell.
Registering their address at the property for municipal tax purposes.
Inviting relatives to stay at the property.
answer: Making structural alterations to the property with the explicit permission of the owner pursuant to the agreement to sell.
explanation: If a transferee is already in possession, Section 53A requires them to do 'some other act in furtherance of the contract'. Simply continuing possession or paying rent relates to the old tenancy. Making structural alterations pursuant to the sale agreement is an independent act referable unequivocally to the new contract.
trick: Pre-existing Possession Trap: If already a tenant, mere continuation of possession fails S.53A. The act must be unequivocally linked to the *sale* contract, not the tenancy.
tip: Transferee already in possession must do an independent act referable to the sale contract.

question: Assertion (A): Section 41 (Ostensible Owner) places the burden of proof entirely on the real owner to prove that the transferee acted in bad faith. Reason (R): Equity favors the bona fide purchaser over a negligent real owner who allowed another to appear as the owner.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: A is false but R is true
explanation: Assertion (A) is false. Under Section 41, the burden of proof is strictly on the TRANSFEREE to prove that they acted in good faith and took reasonable care to ascertain the transferor's power. It is a statutory exception to the rule 'nemo dat quod non habet', so the party seeking its protection must prove compliance.
trick: Burden of Proof Trap: The burden is always on the transferee asserting S.41, not the real owner defending their title.
tip: The burden of proving good faith and reasonable care under S.41 rests on the transferee.

question: A suit for specific performance is filed in a court in Delhi regarding property located entirely in Mumbai. During the pendency of this suit, the defendant sells the Mumbai property to X. Does Section 52 apply to void the sale to X?
options: Yes, because a suit was actively pending between the parties.
No, because the Delhi court lacked territorial jurisdiction over the immovable property, making the suit jurisdictionally defective.
Yes, because specific performance is an action in personam that can be filed anywhere.
No, because Section 52 requires the suit to be filed in the High Court.
answer: No, because the Delhi court lacked territorial jurisdiction over the immovable property, making the suit jurisdictionally defective.
explanation: Section 52 explicitly requires that the suit or proceeding must be pending in a Court having authority 'within the limits of India'. Jurisprudence dictates that the court MUST have competent territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction over the subject matter. A suit filed in a court completely lacking territorial jurisdiction over the immovable property does not trigger Lis Pendens.
trick: Jurisdiction Trap: Lis pendens strictly requires pendency in a 'competent' court. A jurisdictionally void suit cannot freeze alienation rights.
tip: Lis pendens requires the pending suit to be in a court of competent jurisdiction.

question: In the context of Section 43, what happens if the transferor, who initially had no title, acquires the title, but before the transferee exercises his option to claim the property, the transferor goes bankrupt and the property vests in the Official Receiver?
options: The transferee can still exercise the option and take the property from the Official Receiver.
The transferee loses the right because the property vests in the Receiver free from personal equitable estoppels.
The transferee gets a 50% equitable share.
The transferee must file a fresh suit under Section 41.
answer: The transferee loses the right because the property vests in the Receiver free from personal equitable estoppels.
explanation: Section 43 creates an equity that binds the transferor. However, if the property passes to a bona fide purchaser or an Official Receiver/Assignee in bankruptcy before the option is exercised, the equity is cut off. The Official Receiver represents the creditors and takes the property free from unexercised personal estoppels.
trick: Bankruptcy Trap: The option under S.43 must be exercised while the transferor still holds the acquired title. Intervening bankruptcy cuts off the transferee's equitable claim.
tip: Unexercised S.43 option is defeated by the transferor's intervening bankruptcy/Official Receiver vesting.

question: Assertion (A): A plaintiff suing in forma pauperis (indigent person) files the application to sue on Jan 1. The application is admitted and numbered as a suit on March 1. The defendant sells the property on Feb 1. Section 52 applies to this sale. Reason (R): The Explanation to Section 52 states that the pendency of a suit commences from the date of the presentation of the plaint or the institution of the proceeding.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
explanation: For an indigent person, the presentation of the application for leave to sue in forma pauperis is deemed to be the institution of the suit. Therefore, lis pendens commences from Jan 1 (presentation), not March 1 (admission). The sale on Feb 1 is hit by Section 52.
trick: Pauper Suit Trap: Pendency starts when the application to sue as an indigent is *presented*, not when it is formally registered as a suit after inquiry.
tip: In pauper suits, Lis Pendens commences upon the presentation of the application to sue.

question: A signs a written agreement to sell a house to B. B takes possession but only pays 10% advance. The agreement contains no specific details about the remaining payment schedule or the exact dimensions of the property. A attempts to evict B. Can B use Section 53A?
options: Yes, because taking possession is the paramount requirement.
No, because the contract lacks ascertainable terms necessary to constitute a valid agreement under Section 53A.
Yes, because the 10% payment establishes willingness to perform.
No, because Section 53A only applies if 50% or more consideration is paid.
answer: No, because the contract lacks ascertainable terms necessary to constitute a valid agreement under Section 53A.
explanation: Section 53A requires a contract in writing 'from which the terms necessary to constitute the transfer can be ascertained with reasonable certainty'. If fundamental terms like boundaries and payment schedules are vague or missing, the document fails the statutory threshold for Part Performance.
trick: Certainty Trap: Mere written paper + possession isn't enough. The contract must be clear and specific enough to be theoretically enforceable in specific performance.
tip: S.53A requires the written contract's terms to be ascertainable with reasonable certainty.

question: Under Section 52 (Lis Pendens), what is the legal effect if the plaintiff and defendant enter into a bona fide compromise decree rather than fighting the suit to the end?
options: Lis pendens ceases to apply because compromise decrees are essentially private contracts.
Lis pendens applies to the compromise decree, and the pendente lite transferee is bound by its terms.
The compromise decree is void if a pendente lite transfer occurred before it.
Lis pendens applies only if the transferee consents to the compromise.
answer: Lis pendens applies to the compromise decree, and the pendente lite transferee is bound by its terms.
explanation: The Supreme Court has held that a compromise decree (passed under Order 23 Rule 3 CPC) is a decree within the meaning of Section 52. As long as the compromise was bona fide and not collusive, the pendente lite transferee is bound by the terms of the compromise decree just as they would be by a contested decree.
trick: Compromise Decree Trap: Transferees often argue they shouldn't be bound by a secret deal between the parties. However, unless they prove collusion/fraud, a compromise decree binds them under S.52.
tip: A bona fide compromise decree strictly binds a pendente lite transferee under S.52.

question: X, a coparcener in a Hindu Joint Family, sells a specific plot of joint family land to Y without the consent of the other coparceners. Later, a partition takes place, and that exact plot falls into X's share. Y invokes Section 43. Does it apply?
options: No, because Joint Hindu Family properties are governed exclusively by personal law, not the TPA.
No, because a coparcener has no specific title to any property before partition.
Yes, Section 43 applies, and Y can compel X to deliver the plot since X has now acquired exclusive title to it.
Yes, but Y must pay an additional premium to the Karta.
answer: Yes, Section 43 applies, and Y can compel X to deliver the plot since X has now acquired exclusive title to it.
explanation: This is a classic application of Section 43. Although X had no right to alienate a specific item of joint family property before partition, once he erroneously/fraudulently purported to do so, and later acquired exclusive title to it upon partition, equity compels him to 'feed the grant' to Y.
trick: Coparcenary Partition Trap: Before partition, a coparcener has no exclusive right. Post-partition acquisition is treated exactly as 'subsequently acquiring title' under S.43.
tip: S.43 applies when an alienating coparcener is allotted the alienated property upon partition.

question: Assertion (A): If the transferor acquires the title to the property but the transferee had already rescinded the contract of sale, the transferee can later change their mind and claim the property under Section 43. Reason (R): Section 43 imposes an absolute statutory obligation on the transferor that cannot be extinguished by the transferee's actions.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are false
explanation: Section 43 explicitly states that the transfer operates at the option of the transferee, provided the contract of transfer 'subsists'. If the transferee discovers the defect in title and rescinds (cancels) the contract before the transferor acquires title, the contract no longer subsists. The transferee cannot revive a dead contract to claim S.43.
trick: Subsisting Contract Trap: The estoppel relies on a live contract. Rescission kills the contract and destroys the S.43 option forever.
tip: S.43 option fails if the transferee rescinds the contract before the title is acquired.

question: Which of the following scenarios fails the 'Reasonable Care' test required by a transferee under Section 41 (Ostensible Owner)?
options: Searching the sub-registrar's office for prior encumbrances.
Relying solely on revenue records (Jamabandi/Khatauni) while ignoring that someone else is in physical possession of the property.
Publishing a public notice in two local newspapers regarding the intent to purchase.
Engaging an advocate to verify the chain of title deeds over the last 12 years.
answer: Relying solely on revenue records (Jamabandi/Khatauni) while ignoring that someone else is in physical possession of the property.
explanation: Courts hold that mere reliance on revenue/mutation records does not constitute 'reasonable care' under Section 41, especially because mutation does not confer title. Furthermore, if a third party is in actual physical possession, the buyer has a duty to inquire about the nature of that possession. Ignoring physical possession is fatal to the 'reasonable care' defense.
trick: Mutation Trap: Revenue entries are for tax purposes, not title. A buyer who doesn't physically inspect the property fails the S.41 diligence test.
tip: Relying purely on revenue records while ignoring actual physical possession defeats S.41 good faith.

question: Section 52 (Lis Pendens) applies to execution proceedings (involuntary sales) under the Civil Procedure Code. Which landmark Supreme Court judgment solidified this rule, ending the debate that S.52 only applies to voluntary acts of parties?
options: Kedar Nath v. Sheo Haldar
Samarendra Nath Sinha v. Krishna Kumar Nag
Rameshwar v. Jot Ram
Jayaram Mudaliar v. Ayyaswami
answer: Samarendra Nath Sinha v. Krishna Kumar Nag
explanation: In 'Samarendra Nath Sinha v. Krishna Kumar Nag', the Supreme Court clarified that the doctrine of lis pendens applies equally to involuntary alienations, such as court sales in execution of decrees, as it does to voluntary alienations by the parties.
trick: Voluntary/Involuntary Trap: The wording of S.52 ('transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party') seems to imply voluntary action, but SC jurisprudence firmly includes court-ordered execution sales.
tip: Lis pendens applies to involuntary court execution sales (Samarendra Nath Sinha).

question: Assertion (A): Section 53A cannot be used against the transferor if the transferee's right to file a suit for specific performance has become time-barred under the Limitation Act. Reason (R): Section 53A is an equitable remedy, and equity aids the vigilant, not those who sleep on their rights.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
answer: A is false but R is true
explanation: Assertion (A) is false. The Supreme Court in 'Shrimant Shamrao Suryavanshi v. Pralhad Bhairoba Suryavanshi' held that the defense of Part Performance under Section 53A remains available to the transferee even if their right to sue for specific performance has become time-barred. The Limitation Act bars the remedy (sword), but does not extinguish the defensive right (shield). Reason (R) is a general maxim but does not dictate the statutory survival of S.53A.
trick: Limitation Bar Trap: Limitation extinguishes the SWORD (Specific Performance suit), but the SHIELD (S.53A defense to eviction) survives perpetually.
tip: S.53A defense survives even if the limitation period for specific performance has expired.

question: A, lacking title, sells land to B. B later discovers A's lack of title and sues A for the refund of the purchase money. B obtains a decree and recovers the money. Subsequently, A acquires the title to the land. Can B now return the money and invoke Section 43 to claim the land?
options: Yes, because A's subsequent acquisition automatically revives B's option.
No, because by suing for and recovering the purchase money, B has unequivocally rescinded the contract.
Yes, because Section 43 overrides general contract law remedies.
No, because real estate transactions cannot be reversed once money is refunded.
answer: No, because by suing for and recovering the purchase money, B has unequivocally rescinded the contract.
explanation: Section 43 requires the contract of transfer to 'subsist' at the time the transferor acquires the title. By electing to sue for the refund of consideration (damages/rescission), B has permanently terminated the contract. A dead contract cannot be fed by estoppel.
trick: Election of Remedies Trap: The transferee has an option: wait for the title (S.43) OR sue for damages. Choosing damages kills the S.43 option forever.
tip: Suing for refund rescinds the contract, permanently destroying the S.43 option.

question: Which of the following procedural defects in a plaint entirely prevents the doctrine of Lis Pendens (Section 52) from operating?
options: The plaint is insufficiently stamped but later rectified.
The property is vaguely described, making it impossible to identify the specific immovable property in question.
The plaintiff files an amendment to correct a typographical error in the defendant's name.
The suit is transferred from one competent court to another.
answer: The property is vaguely described, making it impossible to identify the specific immovable property in question.
explanation: Section 52 requires that a right to specific immovable property must be 'directly and specifically in question'. If the plaint is so vague that the property cannot be identified, the doctrine fails because third parties have no way of knowing which property is subject to litigation.
trick: Specificity Trap: Misdescription or extreme vagueness defeats S.52 because the 'specifically in question' statutory threshold is not met.
tip: Vague property descriptions in a plaint prevent the application of Lis Pendens.

question: Assertion (A): An unwritten family settlement where possession of property is exchanged cannot be protected under Section 53A. Reason (R): A family settlement is not a 'transfer for consideration' and Section 53A strictly requires a written contract of transfer for consideration.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
explanation: Section 53A explicitly begins with 'Where any person contracts to transfer for consideration any immoveable property by writing...'. A family settlement/partition is jurisprudentially recognized as a rearrangement of pre-existing rights, not a 'transfer'. Furthermore, if unwritten, it fails the 'in writing' test. Hence, S.53A does not apply.
trick: Family Settlement Trap: Partition/family settlements are not 'transfers' under TPA, and S.53A strictly requires a 'transfer for consideration'.
tip: S.53A does not apply to family settlements/partitions as they are not transfers for consideration.

question: A suit for maintenance is filed by a Hindu wife. She prays for a general decree of maintenance against her husband. During the pendency of this suit, the husband sells his house to X. Does Section 52 (Lis Pendens) bind X?
options: Yes, because a wife's maintenance is an automatic charge on all husband's properties.
No, because a general suit for maintenance does not put the title of specific property directly in question.
Yes, because the sale is presumed to be intended to defeat the wife's claim.
No, because Lis Pendens only applies to commercial property disputes.
answer: No, because a general suit for maintenance does not put the title of specific property directly in question.
explanation: A general suit for maintenance does not attract Section 52 because no specific immovable property is in question. However, if the wife prays for a *specific charge* to be created on a *specifically identified house*, then Section 52 would apply to that house.
trick: General vs Specific Charge Trap: A general maintenance claim is personal. It only becomes a S.52 property dispute if a specific charge on specific property is prayed for in the plaint.
tip: General maintenance suits do not trigger S.52 unless a specific charge on property is sought.

question: In the context of Section 41 (Ostensible Owner), the term 'Good Faith' is interpreted according to which statute's definition?
options: The Indian Penal Code, 1860 (done with due care and attention).
The General Clauses Act, 1897 (done honestly, whether negligently or not).
The Limitation Act, 1963.
The Transfer of Property Act has its own explicit internal definition in Section 3.
answer: The Indian Penal Code, 1860 (done with due care and attention).
explanation: Wait, let's be precise. The General Clauses Act defines good faith as 'done honestly, whether negligently or not'. However, for Section 41 TPA, courts have held that the General Clauses Act definition is insufficient because S.41 explicitly adds 'and has taken reasonable care'. Therefore, negligence destroys good faith under S.41, making it akin to the stricter IPC standard (due care and attention) rather than the lenient GCA standard.
trick: Definition Conflict Trap: The GCA allows a negligent act to be in 'good faith'. But S.41 explicitly demands 'reasonable care', meaning negligence kills the S.41 defense entirely.
tip: S.41 good faith strictly requires reasonable care; mere honest negligence is not protected.

question: Assertion (A): Section 43 does not apply to a transfer made by a person who holds the property as a Benamidar for someone else. Reason (R): A Benamidar is an ostensible owner, not someone who erroneously represents having authority, and the real owner's rights are governed by Section 41.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
explanation: Section 43 applies when a person lacks authority but claims to have it. A Benamidar (before the 1988 Act changes) actually had the apparent title with the consent of the real owner, which triggers Section 41 (Ostensible Owner). Section 43 is about unauthorized representation later fed by title; Section 41 is about authorized apparent title.
trick: Doctrinal Overlap Trap: S.41 is for authorized fake owners (benamidar). S.43 is for unauthorized fake owners who later become real owners. They are mutually exclusive.
tip: S.41 deals with apparent title via consent; S.43 deals with false representations of title.

question: A suit is dismissed for default because the plaintiff failed to appear. Two months later, the suit is restored by the court. During the two-month gap between dismissal and restoration, the defendant sells the property to X. Is X bound by Lis Pendens?
options: Yes, because restoration of a suit revives the lis pendens retrospectively.
No, because during the gap, no suit was pending, and the sale is valid and unaffected.
Yes, but only if the plaintiff proves X knew about the restoration application.
No, because dismissal for default completely extinguishes the subject matter.
answer: Yes, because restoration of a suit revives the lis pendens retrospectively.
explanation: Courts (including the Supreme Court) have consistently held that when a suit dismissed for default is restored, the restoration operates retrospectively. The suit is deemed to have been pending continuously. Therefore, alienations made during the gap are hit by Section 52.
trick: Restoration Gap Trap: Logically it seems there is a gap, but the legal fiction of restoration bridges the gap, maintaining the continuity of the lis.
tip: Restoration of a dismissed suit revives Lis Pendens retrospectively over the gap period.

question: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between Section 52 (Lis Pendens) and pre-emption suits?
options: Lis pendens does not apply to pre-emption suits as they restrict free trade.
A sale to a third party during a pre-emption suit is hit by Section 52 and cannot defeat the pre-emptor's right.
Pre-emption suits are exceptions to Section 52 under the Islamic Law of Shufa.
Section 52 only applies if the pre-emptor deposits the full amount before the suit begins.
answer: A sale to a third party during a pre-emption suit is hit by Section 52 and cannot defeat the pre-emptor's right.
explanation: A suit for pre-emption involves a direct claim to immovable property. Therefore, any alienation by the vendee to a third party during the pendency of the pre-emption suit is subject to the doctrine of Lis Pendens, ensuring the pre-emptor's right is not defeated by successive sales.
trick: Pre-emption Trap: The right of pre-emption is a weak right, but once a suit is filed, it firmly attracts S.52 protection against further alienations.
tip: Suits for pre-emption firmly attract the doctrine of Lis Pendens.

question: Assertion (A): Section 53A (Part Performance) can be pleaded as a defense against the Government. Reason (R): Section 53A applies universally to all transfers of immovable property, including those involving the State, as equity binds the Crown.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are false
explanation: Section 53A applies to private contracts. The Supreme Court has held that Section 53A cannot be invoked against the Government regarding government grants or statutory leases, as government property transfers are governed by specific statutes (like the Government Grants Act, 1895) which override the TPA provisions.
trick: Sovereign Immunity Trap: The TPA (and S.53A) generally does not override the Government Grants Act. The State is not bound by this private equitable defense.
tip: Section 53A cannot be used as a defense against the Government under the Government Grants Act.

question: A, expecting to inherit property from his uncle, sells it to B. The uncle dies and leaves the property to his daughter, D. D subsequently sells the property to A. Can B now invoke Section 43 against A?
options: No, because A inherited from D, not directly from the uncle.
Yes, because A ultimately acquired the title, and the source of his acquisition is immaterial for Section 43.
No, because the original transfer was a mere spes successionis, which is permanently void.
Yes, but B must pay A the amount A paid to D.
answer: Yes, because A ultimately acquired the title, and the source of his acquisition is immaterial for Section 43.
explanation: Section 43 applies whenever the transferor 'subsequently acquires any interest in the property'. The exact route or source of the acquisition (whether by direct inheritance, purchase from an heir, or gift) is completely irrelevant. Once A gets the title, equity forces him to feed the grant to B.
trick: Source of Title Trap: The law doesn't care HOW the transferor gets the title. It only cares THAT they got it while the contract still subsists.
tip: Under S.43, the method or source of subsequent title acquisition by the transferor is immaterial.

question: Under Section 52, a suit is deemed to commence from the presentation of the plaint. When does the pendency of the suit legally terminate?
options: On the date the trial court pronounces the judgment.
On the date the final decree or order has been passed.
On the date the decree is completely satisfied or discharged, or the execution becomes time-barred.
On the date the limitation period for filing the first appeal expires, regardless of execution.
answer: On the date the decree is completely satisfied or discharged, or the execution becomes time-barred.
explanation: The Explanation to Section 52 explicitly states that pendency continues until the suit or proceeding has been disposed of by a final decree AND such decree has been completely satisfied or discharged, or its execution has become barred by limitation.
trick: Execution Trap: Pendency doesn't end with the judgment or the appeal. It survives through the execution phase until the decree is fully satisfied.
tip: Pendency continues through execution until the decree is fully satisfied or time-barred.

question: Assertion (A): For Section 41 to apply, the consent of the real owner must be an intentional act designed to deceive the transferee. Reason (R): Ostensible ownership is based on the principle of fraud, requiring active complicity by the real owner.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are false
explanation: Section 41 is based on estoppel by negligence/conduct, not necessarily active fraud. The consent can be merely implied (e.g., standing by while someone else manages and sells your property). Intent to deceive is not a prerequisite; holding someone out as the owner, even carelessly, triggers S.41.
trick: Fraud vs Negligence Trap: S.41 punishes the real owner for their carelessness/inaction in allowing someone else to appear as the owner. Fraud is not required.
tip: S.41 consent can be implied via negligence; an intent to deceive is not required.

question: A, a tenant, signs an agreement to purchase the leased property from his landlord, B. A pays 20% advance but stops paying monthly rent, claiming he is now a purchaser under Section 53A. B sues to evict A for non-payment of rent. Who succeeds?
options: A, because S.53A completely overrides landlord-tenant law upon signing the agreement.
B, because taking an advance does not extinguish the lease; A must prove an independent act in furtherance of the sale contract to alter his status.
A, because paying the 20% advance automatically converts his status from tenant to owner.
B, because agreements to sell between landlords and tenants are void.
answer: B, because taking an advance does not extinguish the lease; A must prove an independent act in furtherance of the sale contract to alter his status.
explanation: When a tenant agrees to buy the property, mere execution of the agreement and payment of earnest money does not automatically end the tenancy. To invoke S.53A, the tenant must show that he was put in possession AS A VENDEE (e.g., stopping rent by mutual agreement, making structural changes). Without this, defaulting on rent justifies eviction.
trick: Dual Status Trap: A tenant remains a tenant until there is a clear, unequivocal act changing the nature of possession from lessee to proposed vendee.
tip: Tenant buying property must show an unequivocal act converting possession status to invoke S.53A.

question: In a dispute, A claims title to a property based on Section 43 against B, while B claims title based on Section 41 as a bona fide purchaser. A's transferor initially had no title but acquired it later. However, the transferor was the ostensible owner when he sold it to B. Which equitable doctrine prevails?
options: Section 43 prevails because subsequent acquisition retroactively validates the first transfer.
Section 41 prevails because it protects the bona fide purchaser against hidden equitable claims.
Both doctrines cancel each other out, and the property reverts to the transferor.
The court will divide the property equally between A and B.
answer: Section 41 prevails because it protects the bona fide purchaser against hidden equitable claims.
explanation: This resolves the intersection of S.41 and S.43. Section 43 expressly contains a proviso: 'Nothing in this section shall impair the right of transferees in good faith for consideration without notice of the existence of the said option'. B is a bona fide purchaser. His rights under S.41/Proviso to S.43 defeat A's unexercised equitable option.
trick: Intersection Trap: A bona fide purchaser for value without notice is the ultimate darling of equity. They defeat almost all prior hidden equities (like S.43 options).
tip: Bona fide purchasers for value without notice defeat prior unexercised S.43 options.

question: Assertion (A): Section 52 requires that a notice of lis pendens must be registered under the Indian Registration Act for the doctrine to affect third-party purchasers. Reason (R): Without registration, a third party has no means of discovering the pending litigation, violating the principles of natural justice.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
answer: Both A and R are false
explanation: Under the Central Transfer of Property Act, 1882, registration of a notice of lis pendens is NOT required. The doctrine operates automatically upon the institution of the suit. (Note: Only a few states like Maharashtra and Gujarat have passed local amendments requiring registration of lis pendens). Both A and R are false as standard central law.
trick: State Amendment Trap: Unless the question specifies Maharashtra/Gujarat, standard TPA S.52 requires ZERO registration. Pendency itself is an absolute bar.
tip: Under central TPA, S.52 operates automatically; registration of lis pendens is not required.

question: Which of the following best describes the doctrine of 'Election' as it intersects with Section 43 (Feeding the Grant)?
options: The transferor must elect whether to feed the grant or pay damages.
The real owner must elect whether to validate the unauthorized transfer or evict the transferee.
The transferee must elect whether to exercise the option to claim the newly acquired title or repudiate the contract.
The court elects the remedy based on the balance of convenience.
answer: The transferee must elect whether to exercise the option to claim the newly acquired title or repudiate the contract.
explanation: Section 43 states the transfer shall operate 'at the option of the transferee'. If the transferor acquires title, the title does not automatically jump to the transferee. The transferee has the election to either claim the property (feed the grant) or repudiate the contract and sue for damages.
trick: Automatic Vesting Trap: The transfer is not automatic. The transferee holds the power of election. If they stay silent, the title remains with the transferor.
tip: S.43 title transfer is not automatic; it requires the transferee to elect/exercise their option.

question: A, a husband, transfers his house to his wife B to protect it from his creditors. B's name is on the title deeds. They divorce. B sells the house to C, who verifies the deeds and buys in good faith. A sues C to recover the house. Does C get protection under Section 41?
options: No, because transfers between spouses are presumed to be for tax evasion, invalidating good faith.
Yes, because A voluntarily made B the ostensible owner with his consent, and C acted in good faith with reasonable care.
No, because the Benami Act makes the initial transfer to B illegal.
Yes, but only if C can prove that A and B were legally divorced at the time of sale.
answer: Yes, because A voluntarily made B the ostensible owner with his consent, and C acted in good faith with reasonable care.
explanation: This is a classic S.41 scenario. A put the property in B's name, giving her implied/express consent to hold herself out as the owner. C, after checking the title deeds (reasonable care) and acting in good faith, purchased it. C is completely protected against A. Furthermore, the Benami Act explicitly exempts property purchased in the name of a spouse from being treated as an illegal benami transaction.
trick: Spousal Exemption Trap: Buying in a wife's name is a legal exception in the Benami Act. Thus, B is a valid ostensible owner, triggering robust S.41 protection for C.
tip: Properties in a spouse's name trigger valid S.41 ostensible ownership against the real owner.
